query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys (LW-HEAs) that solidify as supersaturated single-phase solid solutions, post-solidification ageing at 200–350 °C drives selective outward diffusion of Mg that (i) precipitates nanoscale Mg-rich intermetallics (e.g., C15 Mg2(Al,Cu) Laves) along grain boundaries and (ii) forms an external MgO/Mg(OH)2 layer that rapidly converts to a thin, adherent Al2O3-based inner layer.  This two-step redistribution lowers the Mg activity and the associated galvanic potential differences inside the matrix while simultaneously generating a duplex protective oxide.  The structural/chemical evolution therefore decreases both (a) aqueous corrosion current density and (b) high-temperature (≈600 °C) oxidation mass-gain by ≥30 % relative to the as-cast, non-aged state.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast, induction-melted Mg–Al–Cu–Zn–(rare-earth) lightweight HEA with density < 6 g cm⁻³; nominally single-phase supersaturated solid solution containing 10–20 at.% Mg and minor nanometric quenched-in clusters.
generation.intervention: Isothermal ageing at 250 °C for 24 h in argon (below the onset of bulk recrystallisation).
generation.conditions: Corrosion: 3.5 wt % NaCl solution at 25 °C, open-circuit followed by potentiodynamic polarisation.  High-temperature oxidation: static air at 600 °C for 10 h.
generation.structural_mediator: Precipitation of Mg-rich C15 Laves phase at grain boundaries plus formation of duplex MgO/Al2O3 surface oxide produced by outward‐diffusing Mg.
generation.mechanism: Ageing lowers the chemical potential of Mg in the matrix by (1) exsolving Mg into stable intermetallic precipitates and (2) consuming surface Mg to form MgO, which further enables inward growth of a continuous, slow-growing Al2O3 sub-layer.  Mg depletion suppresses internal micro-galvanic coupling with more noble Cu/Zn/Gd-rich regions, reducing cathodic reaction sites for corrosion; the duplex oxide interrupts outward metal diffusion during high-temperature exposure, decreasing oxidation kinetics.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-cast alloy, the aged alloy will show (a) ≥50 % lower corrosion current density and ≥100 mV higher corrosion potential, and (b) ≥30 % lower parabolic oxidation rate constant over 10 h at 600 °C.
generation.baseline: Same alloy in the non-aged, as-cast supersaturated solid solution state.
generation.boundary: Effect requires ≥8 at.% bulk Mg and ageing temperatures below ~0.5 T_m (≈350 °C).  Ageing above 400 °C or Mg contents <5 at.% will coarsen precipitates or suppress MgO/Al2O3 duplex formation, negating the predicted improvements.
generation.uncertainty: Exact precipitate chemistry and thickness of protective oxides may vary with minor alloying additions; magnitude of corrosion/oxidation improvement may differ (±20 %) depending on surface finish and test environment.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two identical Mg–Al–Cu–Zn–Gd HEA samples (ρ ≈ 4 g cm⁻³).  Keep one as-cast; age the other at 250 °C/24 h in Ar.  Characterise both before testing (XRD, TEM-EDS for precipitates; XPS for surface oxides).  Measure: (i) potentiodynamic polarisation in 3.5 % NaCl; (ii) mass-gain during 600 °C static-air oxidation for 10 h; (iii) post-test SEM/EDS of surfaces and cross-sections.
measurements: Corrosion current density (µA cm⁻²) and corrosion potential (V_SCE)
Parabolic oxidation rate constant k_p (mg² cm⁻⁴ s⁻¹)
TEM-verified volume fraction/size of Mg-rich precipitates
XPS/EDS depth profile of MgO and Al2O3 in the oxide scale
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged sample shows (a) corrosion current density not at least 25 % lower than the as-cast sample OR (b) oxidation k_p not at least 15 % lower, OR if TEM/XPS fail to detect increased Mg-rich precipitates and duplex MgO/Al2O3 scales after ageing, then the hypothesis is falsified.
